lesson.title: Sorting the World Into Boxes: What Data Types Are
lesson.summary: Data types classify every value a program works with, determining what operations are legal and how the value is stored, and Python assigns a type to values rather than to the variable names that point at them.
lesson.body:
Before a computer can add two numbers or join two words, it has to know what kind of thing each value actually is. A data type is a classification that tells the language two things: what values are possible (whole numbers, decimals, text, true or false) and what operations are legal, such as whether two things can be multiplied together or whether that request does not make sense at all. Without types, a computer could not tell the difference between the number 5 and the three characters that spell "five", even though both might be typed the same way on a keyboard.

Python assigns a type to every value the moment it is created, but variables themselves are not locked to a type. This is called dynamic typing. If you write x = 5, Python creates an integer object and points the name x at it. If you later write x = "five", Python creates a brand new string object and repoints x at that instead. The name x never had a type of its own; it just borrows the type of whatever it currently refers to. This is different from languages like Java or C, where you must declare a variable's type up front and it cannot change afterward.

Types matter because operations behave differently, or fail outright, depending on what type they are given. Consider this short trace:

age = 12
name = "Maya"
print(age + 1)
print(name + 1)

The first print works and produces 13, because addition is defined between two integers. The second line raises a TypeError, because Python refuses to guess whether you meant to convert 1 to the string "1" or do something else entirely. Many bugs in real programs come down to exactly this: a value has a different type than the code assumed it would have.

Python organizes values into a handful of core built-in types that you will use constantly: int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, bool for true or false, and str for text. Later lessons in this unit look at each of these individually, along with the type() function that lets you ask Python directly what type a value has, and the conversion functions that let you deliberately change a value from one type to another. Thinking in types, rather than just values, is one of the habits that separates code that happens to work from code you can actually reason about and predict.

It also helps to know that in Python, every single one of these types is itself a full object under the hood, not a special built-in category walled off from the rest of the language. An integer, a string, and a function you define yourself are all objects, which is part of why the same tools, like the type() function covered later, can inspect any of them the same way. This uniformity is a deliberate design choice, and it is one reason Python code tends to look consistent no matter what kind of value you happen to be working with, from a single number up to a complex data structure built out of many of them.
